question: Is making editor.api.history.undo() and redo() uniformly Promise-based the best public contract after fallible external comment replay joined local history?
trigger: The user requested harsh honest feedback on Felix’s newly integrated async undo and redo API before accepting it as the durable history contract.
requirements: Keep one user-visible undo and redo order for successful local comment creation and document edits.
Preserve server-first comment authorization and persistence, typed blocked replay, unchanged branch heads on failure, and no deletion of foreign comment work.
Give every caller one statically honest return type when the current history head may require asynchronous external work.
Avoid conditional timing, silent dropped outcomes, unhandled promise failures, and an invisible editor-wide mutation lock.
Do not add a parallel Comments history stack, a sync-or-Promise union, or separate undo methods whose correct choice depends on the hidden head batch.
evidenceReuse: Rechecked Felix commit 4de58926f2 against its parent, the current Plite History implementation and types, the mounted React replay owner, native shortcut adapters, the Comments server-first mutation owner, current docs, focused session-effect tests, production caller census, the TaskHub 22 execution plan, and the prior history ownership records. Reused existing green correctness proof only for branch ordering, blocking and focus; it does not prove API timing or pending-interaction quality. A bounded local comparison with the checked-out Slate and Lexical histories confirmed their synchronous document-only replay but is not decisive because they do not own Plate’s fallible external session effect job.
summary: Pursue a replay-lifecycle redesign while retaining Promise<HistoryResult> as the public undo and redo return type. The Promise is the only honest single signature once one history head may await server-first comment mutation; restoring sync, returning a sync-or-Promise union, splitting undo methods, or removing comment creation from the shared order all lose a stated requirement. The current implementation is still not a best API: ordinary replay mutates before returning Promise.resolve while session replay crosses an await, native callers commonly discard the result, and session replay globally rejects editor publication without exposing pending state. A slow provider can therefore create an invisible locked editor and a blocked shortcut result with no consumer. The durable target is one uniformly scheduled replay queue with observable pending direction/state, mounted input and controls owned by that lifecycle, and explicit blocked/error handling; the detailed concurrency contract must decide whether interaction is disabled, buffered, or safely cancelled before implementation.

reconciliation.question: After accounting for Plate descriptor structure and types, should Plite gain native configuration so the Plate history state/getter adapter can disappear?
reconciliation.reason: Felix’s later session-effect work changes replay timing and public completion semantics, which the configuration review never assessed. Its Stop conclusion about the Plate configuration adapter remains intact outside this newly opened replay-lifecycle question.

alternatives: Keep the current Promise signature and implementation unchanged: rejected because it has synchronous and asynchronous observation timing under one return type, silently discarded native outcomes, and no public pending state despite an editor-wide publication fence.

Restore synchronous undo and redo: rejected because server-first comment replay can reject or await network work before the branch may safely move; synchronous success would lie or require unsafe optimistic compensation.

Return HistoryResult | Promise<HistoryResult>, or add undoSync and undoAsync: rejected because callers must know the hidden top-batch kind before choosing or narrowing the API, spreading history internals through every consumer.
Remove comment creation from editor history or add a Comments-only stack: rejected because it loses the requested A/B/C user order or creates two competing shortcut owners.

Make Comments local-first and persist after synchronous replay: viable only as a different product contract. It removes the async requirement by abandoning server-first canonical publication and must not be imposed on applications that require authorization before local publication.

Retain Promise<HistoryResult> and redesign one replay lifecycle: strongest target. Schedule all replay through one queue, expose pending direction/state, make mounted input and controls honor it, and ensure blocked/error outcomes are consumed. Keep the branch and external mutation atomic under an explicit concurrency policy.
proofLimits: Source and contract review only. Existing tests prove comment order, blocked branch retention, queue serialization and one Chromium focus route; they do not simulate slow network persistence followed by typing, toolbar actions, editor retirement, rejection surfaced through native shortcuts, or unhandled replay errors. No product code, test, benchmark or browser run was added in this review. The exact pending-state shape and whether later interaction is disabled, buffered or cancelled remain design questions. The Promise verdict assumes the current server-first Comments contract and shared A/B/C order remain hard requirements.
